thread.title_full: Tampa volleyball scion Kyle Dagostino holds tight to Olympic dream - NewsBreak

author: Tampa Bay Times
title: Tampa volleyball scion Kyle Dagostino holds tight to Olympic dream - NewsBreak
text:
10 hours ago The United States' Kyle Dagostino celebrates during a Volleyball Nations League match against Canada in June in Hoffman Estates, Illinois. At age 30, he continues to pursue his dream of landing a spot on the U.S. 12-man Olympic team. [ DANIEL BARTEL | USA Volleyball/Daniel Bartel ] TAMPA — Volleyball has taken Kyle Dagostino all over the world.
He played collegiately at Stanford, where he capped off a five-year career with All-America honors in 2019; professionally across Europe; and internationally with the U.S. men’s national team, everywhere from Brazil to the Philippines, where the world championships end on Sunday.
No matter how far he goes, Dagostino maintains none of it would be possible without his support system back home in Tampa.
Dagostino’s parents are volleyball pioneers in the region.
His mother, Lauri, played at USF; his father, Randy, led Berkeley Prep to 15 state girls championships and a boys title in 2014 with Kyle as his star player. Three of the girls championships were won with his daughter, Mackenzie, who went on to become a two-time All America setter at Florida.
“My parents weren’t instrumental so much as they were the instrument,” Dagostino said.
Kyle Dagostino helped out on his dad's sideline years before he'd lead the charge to a state championship himself. [ Courtesy of Lauri and Randy Dagostino ] Lauri and Randy started the first travel volleyball club in Florida in 1984 and now organize major youth tournaments in Washington D.C., Atlanta and New Orleans while still residing in Tampa. Mackenzie and her husband contribute, too.
Dagostino took after them from a young age and never looked back. He’s accomplished more than ever could have been imagined when he was a 7-year-old playing for his sister’s team that was all girls otherwise.
Still, Dagostino says, he is too stubborn to be satisfied. His journey, and the village that has made it possible, motivate him as he chases his childhood dream of becoming an Olympian.
“It’s a dream that I want to fulfill not just for myself, but also for my family,” Dagostino, 30, said from Los Angeles, where the national team trains. “We’ve poured so many resources into getting me to this point. I feel, and they would probably disagree with me, this is something I want and need to do for them as much as I want to do it for myself.”
Learning by ‘osmosis’ Kyle, left, and Randy Dagostino pose with the trophy after Berkeley Prep won a boys volleyball state championship in 2014. [ Courtesy of Lauri and Randy Dagostino ] The year was 1983, and Berkeley Prep needed a volleyball coach.
Randy, the school’s athletic director at the time, spent six months leading a fruitless search. Left without options, he started reading volleyball books and attending coaching clinics. Randy, a collegiate baseball player, coached the women’s team that year and never looked back.
Berkeley Prep grew into a powerhouse that produced collegiate players and won state championships essentially every other year for nearly three decades.
“We are a volleyball family through and through, and I would have never said that was going to happen when it first started,” Randy said.
Kyle, born in 1995, was around volleyball long before there were boy’s teams for him to play on. Even as a toddler, he had a volleyball in his hands. His parents, despite their pedigree, take little credit for his skills. They say he basically taught himself how to play.
“Kyle was a learn-by-osmosis kind of kid,” Lauri said.
Kyle Dagostino had a volleyball in his hands even as a toddler. His parents say he basically taught himself how to play. [ Courtesy of Lauri and Randy Dagostino ] Dagostino’s first club team experiences were alongside his older sister, before his parents were able to recruit enough boys to form a team. Once they did, those teams were successful in national tournaments, and Dagostino, who primarily played setter, caught the attention of some of the country’s best collegiate programs.
These schools, however, were recruiting him to play the defensive specialist position of libero. At 5 feet 9, Dagostino was not considered tall enough to play in the front row, where he would be responsible for blocking attackers, some nearly a foot taller than him.
He tried his hardest to convince college coaches to take him as a setter, but none of the high-caliber programs that were recruiting him — UCLA, Stanford, Pepperdine and Loyola-Chicago — budged.
“I would still say my heart is as a setter, but I have come to terms over the years with being a libero,” Dagostino said.
Dagostino set his sights on Stanford as a middle schooler, so it was not too difficult of a choice when the Cardinal came calling.
“If I set myself up to go to a school like Stanford and it ended up not working out but I was doing everything that I could to get there, then I would probably have a really good opportunity to go just about anywhere else,” Dagostino said.
Kyle Dagostino, left, with his sister, Mackenzie. Both were part of state championship teams at Berkeley Prep. [ Courtesy of Lauri and Randy Dagostino ] He sacrificed his preferred position for the opportunity to play at his dream school and give himself a chance at his Olympic dream afterwards. Or so he thought.
His college coach called Dagostino the summer before his freshman year and offered him the opportunity to set. Stanford’s starting setter needed knee surgery, its backup quit and its third-string setter had to go home for personal reasons.
Dagostino got to make 15 starts at setter that year, though the original starter’s return gradually cut his playing time and put him back on a track where his best prospects were at libero. He redshirted as a senior — still committed to pursuing volleyball after college — and took the year to learn the libero position.
He returned the next year and earned All-American honors as a libero, a season worthy of the national team’s attention, especially because Dagostino performed particularly well against UCLA, coached at the time by the national team’s head coach.
Professional journey, Olympic dream Kyle Dagostino attempts a kick save during a Volleyball Nations League match. [ Courtesy of USA Volleyball; Photo by Volleyball World ] Success as a college player is only a fraction of the battle. Some Division I stars never receive an invite to practice with the national team, while plenty of others last only a summer or two.
Dagostino got his opportunity before he even graduated, though he also experienced how fleeting it can be. He was rostered for the Volleyball Nations League tournament in 2019 and had to finish his Stanford courses away from campus while he trained.
The national team exposure earned him his first professional contract in the fall with a Slovenian team that competes in the Champions League, a tournament featuring the best pro teams in the world.
“I don’t know how many liberos coming out of the States get to play in the Champions League in their first year, but I was lucky enough to have that chance,” Dagostino said.
He signed to play in Frankfurt, Germany, the next year but quickly transferred back to Slovenia for a second season. The delayed Tokyo Olympics took place that summer, but Dagostino was not selected for the training group, which affected his search for his next contract. Libero is widely considered the hardest position for an American player to find an overseas contract.
Dagostino was coaching at Pepperdine when a Finnish team offered him a contract in November 2021. He went from Malibu to Finland in less than a week and has had better luck finding contracts since then. He played two seasons in France and soon will start his second season with Berlin Recycling Volleys, the German Bundesliga’s premier club.
“There’s pressure to perform and to execute,” Dagostino said. “It’s a culture that is built on winning titles.”
The expectations, Dagostino noted, come with a reputation that has helped him remain squarely in the mix with the national team. He is one of only two liberos on the world championship roster, and he’s even recently represented the U.S. as a team captain in some instances. When the national team won the bronze medal at the 2024 Olympics, he was one of three alternates watching from the stands.
Kyle Dagostino, second from right, celebrates during a match at the 2024 Paris Olympics. He was one of three alternates watching from the stands as the United States won the bronze medal. [ Courtesy of USA Volleyball; Photo by Volleyball World ] “(The Olympics) were remarkable, even though it was kind of a secondary perspective,” Dagostino said. “It’s a hard thing to describe. It really is the pinnacle of the sport in the world.”
“If that ends up being my only (Olympic) experience in my life, I won’t forget what that felt like and what it was like to have been there.”
Dagostino has effectively accomplished it all as a member of the national team, but a spot on the Olympic 12 eludes him, as it does for most liberos. The U.S. typically only carries one, while every other position group has multiple players selected. That’s why Dagostino was in Paris but not in uniform — in case of emergency.
The position typically only opens up generationally. This generation’s libero is Erik Shoji, who will be 38 when the 2028 Los Angeles Games start and has a strong shot at making his fourth Olympics team.
Kyle Dagostino is pictured during media day for the U.S. men's national team in May. He has accomplished just about everything as a member of the national team, though a spot on the Olympic 12 eludes him. [ DON LIEBIG | USA Volleyball ] Dagostino, who will be 33 when the 2028 Games begin, is committed to trying to make the roster, even if he’s fighting an uphill battle.
“Maybe I’m just a little bit more stubborn than some of the other guys that have been in similar positions as I’ve been over the past few years,” Dagostino said. “I don’t want to give in.
“Seeing how I’ve developed as a professional player, I think I’m playing some great volleyball over these last couple of years. And I think that the gap is closing between he and I, and I’m just hoping for the opportunity at this point to show the staff and my team that I can do this job as well. It’s going to be a little bit different, but I can perform at a high level consistently as well.”
Still, it’s not an objective that will define his career. Volleyball has given the Dagostinos far more than any title or medal could. His parents recount watching their son play with confidence and joy in front of thousands as incredibly proud memories, and he cherishes the familial bond the sport has facilitated.
“(Volleyball) was something that all of us shared, but it wasn’t just something that all of us shared a small interest in,” Dagostino said. “It was what we all were passionate about at the same time. Volleyball was the glue that brought us together to be as close as we are.”
